text:
Why It Matters

The Love Lives On Act of 2025 cleared the House Veterans' Affairs disability-assistance subcommittee on March 26, and its Senate companion, S. 410, was ordered reported favorably by the Senate Veterans' Affairs Committee on March 18. The bill would bar remarriage from ending dependency and indemnity compensation, special pension benefits, or Survivor Benefit Plan annuities for surviving spouses of deceased service members or veterans, and would expand TRICARE eligibility to certain remarried widows and widowers. The Military Officers Association of America (MOAA) lobbied H.R. 1004 in its third-quarter 2026 report, and the House bill is in committee. ​

By the Numbers

MOAA's third-quarter 2026 report discloses $1,070,863 in lobbying spending, up $216,476 from the second quarter of 2026. Spending is up $647,884 from $422,979 in the third quarter of 2025. MOAA lobbies entirely in-house. The filing names 10 lobbyists: Brenden McMahon, René Campos, Jen Goodale, Karen Ruedisueli, Terry Waters, Brian Kelly, April Vogel, Stephanie Rose, Susie Dunham, and Jim O'Brien III.

Broader Context

H.R. 1004 was introduced Feb. 5, 2025, by Rep. Richard Hudson (R-NC-9); S. 410 was introduced by Sen. Jerry Moran (R-KS). The House bill had 139 cosponsors as of the filing date. The Tragedy Assistance Program for Survivors (TAPS) reported that more than 50 veteran and military organizations support the bill; TAPS president Bonnie Carroll said surviving spouses should not have to choose between finding love again and financial security, citing Department of Veterans Affairs data showing roughly 506,000 dependency and indemnity compensation recipients. At a Feb. 24 bipartisan Veterans Service Organization hearing, House Veterans' Affairs Committee Ranking Member Mark Takano cited the Love Lives On Act as one of his legislative priorities.

The Veterans' Assuring Critical Care Expansions to Support Servicemembers (ACCESS) Act, H.R. 740, was introduced Jan. 28, 2025, by Rep. Mike Bost (R-IL-12). It would codify access standards for the Veterans Community Care Program (VCCP), require the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) to notify veterans of care eligibility within two business days, and create an online self-service appointment module. House Veterans' Affairs Committee Democrats argued the bill would widen private-provider access without equivalent oversight and could allow veterans to bypass available VA appointments.

The Military Spouse Hiring Act, H.R. 2033, was introduced March 11, 2025, by Rep. Donald S. Beyer, Jr. (D-VA-8) and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee. It would extend the federal Work Opportunity Tax Credit (WOTC) to employers who hire certified spouses of active-duty service members. More than two dozen organizations, including the Wounded Warrior Project and The American Legion, backed the Military Spouse Hiring Act in March 2025.

Competitive Landscape

Disabled American Veterans is among the organizations associated with the Love Lives On Act. Nine organizations are tied to the Veterans' ACCESS Act, including Document Storage Systems Inc., Disabled American Veterans, Wounded Warrior Project Inc., Mission Roll Call, and Zeel Networks Inc.

The Bottom Line

The Love Lives On Act was forwarded from the House Veterans' Affairs disability-assistance subcommittee to the full committee on March 26, 2026, and its Senate companion, S. 410, was ordered reported favorably by the Senate Veterans' Affairs Committee on March 18, 2026. The House bill, H.R. 740, is listed as in committee, and the record does not show later committee or floor action on it or on its Senate companion, S. 275. H.R. 2033 has the status "Introduced," and its latest recorded action is referral to the House Committee on Ways and Means. Across complete quarters in the evidence, MOAA's in-house team shrank by one lobbyist from the prior quarter as spending reached its highest recorded level.

text:
CLARKSVILLE, TN (CLARKSVILLE NOW) – Premier Medical Group, a multi-physician medical practice based in Clarksville, has agreed to pay $2.8 million to resolve allegations that it violated the False Claims Act by improperly billing Medicare and TRICARE for services provided by non-physician practitioners.

Premier has stated the dispute was over a coding issue that it discovered, self-reported and resolved several years ago. “This matter is related solely to a coding issue. It does not involve any concerns related to the quality of care provided by our team, and no patient or payer was billed for a service that was not provided,” said a statement Premier shared with Clarksville Now on Tuesday.

The settlement resolves allegations that, from Nov. 1, 2018, through May 31, 2023, Premier submitted claims to Medicare and TRICARE for services performed by non-physician practitioners using physicians’ National Provider Identifier (NPI) numbers, according to a news release from the U.S. Attorney’s Office, Middle District of Tennessee.

“Federal health care programs depend on providers following the rules and billing taxpayers accurately,” said U.S. Attorney Braden H. Boucek. “When providers submit improper claims, they undermine the integrity of programs that millions of Americans, including our service members and veterans, rely on for essential care. Our office will continue working with our law enforcement partners to protect these programs and ensure that taxpayer dollars are spent as intended.”

Under the terms of the settlement agreement, Premier will pay $2.8 million to the United States.

“We opted to settle this matter rather than take on the distraction and expense of a long court process,” the Premier statement said. “Notably, we have not agreed that any wrongdoing has occurred, and we are not being required to enter into a corporate integrity agreement or action plan to remedy any concerns about our conduct or operations.

“We are pleased to have this matter behind us and to be able to focus all of our time and attention on helping our team care for this community each day,” the statement said.

title: Judge peels apart protests against DHA's $1.6B health readiness award
description:
On one hand, a federal judge’s ruling to deny two protests against the Defense Health Agency’s selection of Optum's federal-facing subsidiary for a $1.6 billion health readiness contract is a normal part of the legal process.
Judge Zachary Somers decided to use that illustration in his 35-page ruling against the protests filed by LTS Health Partners and incumbent QTC Medical Services, a subsidiary of Leidos, against the award to OptumServe Health Services.
The protests were filed in May and denied on Oct. 9, while the ruling was unsealed on Oct. 28.
The fourth bidder’s identity is redacted from the public version of Somers’ ruling.
Optum was given a “Substantial” rating for past performance, which the court ruling indicates is a major factor in what swung the award.
text:
On one hand, a federal judge’s ruling to deny two protests against the Defense Health Agency’s selection of Optum's federal-facing subsidiary for a $1.6 billion health readiness contract is a normal part of the legal process.

But on the other hand: it is not often that a Court of Federal Claims decision compares a protest to how people use lint rollers to remove pet hair and other small fibers from clothing.

Judge Zachary Somers decided to use that illustration in his 35-page ruling against the protests filed by LTS Health Partners and incumbent QTC Medical Services, a subsidiary of Leidos, against the award to OptumServe Health Services. The protests were filed in May and denied on Oct. 9, while the ruling was unsealed on Oct. 28.

Somers’ introduction compared the protesters’ approach to how all capable lawyers can find problems in any government procurement, much like how lint rollers can pick up anything.

The problem for all protesters, including these two, is that it is not enough to merely point out mistakes an agency made in a procurement and count the number of errors. Protesters must instead show the errors have “some significance.”

Enter Somers with a colorful summary of how, in his eyes, LHP and QTC ignored that basic principle:

“Deploying a total of (17) arguments across approximately 150 pages of briefing, plaintiffs have done their best impression of a lint roller, attempting to pick every particle off this procurement.”

DHA awarded the Remote Health Reserve Program-4th Generation Support Services contract to OptumServe Health Services in April over three other proposals, including those from QTC and LTS. The fourth bidder’s identity is redacted from the public version of Somers’ ruling.

There was some disagreement among the key decision makers on who to choose for the contract. QTC was the source selection authority council’s recommended awardee, but the council’s report did spell out dissenting opinions from two members that Optum should win instead.

The source selection authority was not obligated to follow the council recommendations and ratings to the proposals, but he followed most of them.

He did assign QTC a lower past performance confidence rating than the council recommended, from Substantial to Satisfactory. LHP was upgraded from Limited to Neutral, but only on the lack of available information.

Optum was given a “Substantial” rating for past performance, which the court ruling indicates is a major factor in what swung the award. Optum also had the advantage in the Technical/Risk factor over QTC.

But did DHA actually make any mistakes that meet the legal threshold to win a protest in court? Were DHA’s actions, findings and conclusions in fact arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with the law?

Even if the answer to those questions is yes, protesters still have to spell out all of their arguments as to why and essentially help the judge follow along as they make them.

Each and every section of the ruling’s analysis section begins with some variation of “Failed to show,” whether the judge addresses an individual protester or them as a pair.

The court deferred to how DHA evaluated past performance as a matter of precedent, meaning the plaintiffs had to detail their arguments.

“Neither plaintiff even made it to base camp,” Somers wrote.

Somers summarized the protesters’ arguments as “half-developed” and suggested that future litigants read his decision in detail as a reminder that they are much better off with “carefully selecting and fully developing a few key arguments.”

Nowhere in his ruling does Somers appear to have found an error by DHA that prejudiced either LHP or QTC from the award. DHA seems to have done its homework in defending its choice of Optum over the others.

Somers also used the classic kitchen sink imagery to make his point that these protests fell well short of the mark:

“Plaintiffs threw everything they could think of at the court in hopes that something would stick. They came up empty.”

Back to the beginning with a second main takeaway from this one: lint rollers may be valuable tools in life, but are not in the courts and certainly not when trying to get a contract award vacated.

text:
Seeking Mental Health Care With TRICARE or VA Benefits

Category: Uncategorized | Last Updated: November 1, 2026

Written By: MHH

If you’re seeking mental health care with TRICARE or VA benefits, here’s how to check eligibility, understand potential costs and take the first step.

Key Takeaways

TRICARE is health insurance from the Department of Defense. VA health care is a care system run by the Department of Veterans Affairs. Which one you can use for mental health care depends on your military status: Active duty families and retirees typically have TRICARE, veterans who didn’t retire may qualify for VA health care and some people qualify for both. Some VA mental health services, including emergency suicide care and Vet Centers, don’t require VA enrollment at all.

If you’ve served or you love someone who has, getting mental health care can feel like it starts with a paperwork puzzle. Is it TRICARE or the VA? Do you need a referral? Are you even still covered? Those questions stop a lot of people before they ever book a first appointment.

Much of what you’ll read online starts with the plan and skips the question that actually decides your options: your military status. This guide starts there. Find your situation in the table below, see where your coverage most likely comes from and take the first step that fits.

TRICARE vs. VA: Two Different Kinds of Coverage

It helps to know that TRICARE and the VA don’t work the same way, even though people often lump them together as “military insurance.”

TRICARE Is Insurance

It's the Department of Defense health plan, and it pays for care from military hospitals and clinics and from civilian providers in its network. It covers active duty service members, their families, military retirees and some Guard and Reserve members.

VA Health Care Is a Care System

The Department of Veterans Affairs runs its own medical centers, clinics and Vet Centers and, in some cases, pays for community providers. It serves eligible veterans. It isn't insurance, and it generally doesn't cover veterans' family members.

One of the most common misunderstandings is that TRICARE covers veterans in general. Most veterans who separate without retiring aren’t eligible for TRICARE. For them, the VA is usually the main path to mental health care.

Which Coverage Applies to You?

Start with the row that matches your situation. Eligibility rules have exceptions and can change, so treat this as a starting point and confirm the details with TRICARE or the VA.

Your situationWhere mental health coverage usually comes fromYour first stepActive duty service memberTRICARE, at no cost to youGo to the mental health clinic at your military hospital or clinic, or talk with your primary care manager about a referral for civilian care.Spouse or child of an active duty memberTRICARE Prime or TRICARE SelectLook for a network mental health provider through TRICARE’s provider directory or your regional contractor.National Guard or Reserve memberActive duty TRICARE coverage while on qualifying orders; otherwise, TRICARE Reserve Select if you’ve purchased itCheck your current coverage in milConnect. You may also be eligible for Vet Center services.Leaving the military without retiringUp to 180 days of transitional TRICARE coverage if you qualify, then VA health care if you’re eligibleConfirm your transitional coverage in milConnect before you separate, and apply for VA health care early.Military retiree, including medical retirementTRICARE, plus VA health care if you qualifyConsider enrolling in both. Use the VA for service-connected conditions and TRICARE for other care.Veteran who separated without retiringVA health care (usually not TRICARE)Apply for VA health care online or by phone, or visit a Vet Center, which doesn’t require enrollment.Spouse or child of a veteran with a permanent and total service-connected disability, or who died from a service-connected conditionCHAMPVA, if you don’t qualify for TRICAREApply for CHAMPVA through the VA.

If you’re a military spouse or family member, our guide to support for military families covers resources built for you.

Getting Mental Health Care With TRICARE

TRICARE covers a broad range of mental health services when they’re medically or psychologically necessary, including outpatient therapy, psychiatric care, medication management, intensive outpatient programs, partial hospitalization programs and inpatient care. It also covers treatment for substance use disorders.

The rules that trip people up are referrals and pre-authorization. Some websites still say every TRICARE member needs a referral for therapy, which isn’t accurate. Here’s what TRICARE’s own guidance says.

Before Your First Therapy Appointment

Active duty service members need a referral and pre-authorization for mental health care from a civilian network provider. You don’t need one for outpatient mental health care at a military hospital or clinic.

TRICARE Prime enrollees who aren’t on active duty, such as family members, don’t need a referral for most office-based outpatient therapy with a network provider. Psychoanalysis and outpatient therapy for substance use disorders are exceptions.

TRICARE Select enrollees can see any TRICARE-authorized provider for most outpatient care without a referral. Seeing a non-network provider usually costs more.

Everyone on TRICARE needs pre-authorization for nonemergency inpatient mental health care. Some other services, such as psychoanalysis, also require pre-authorization.

When you call a provider, ask whether they’re in the TRICARE network before you book. Our guide to finding therapy your insurance covers has more questions worth asking.

Getting Mental Health Care Through the VA

VA mental health care covers conditions such as PTSD, depression, anxiety and substance use disorders through VA medical centers, outpatient clinics, telehealth and community Vet Centers. For most ongoing care, the first step is applying for VA health care. After you enroll, the VA assigns you to a priority group based on factors like your service history, disability rating and income, which affects what you pay.

Cost is often lower than people expect. Care for a service-connected condition is free. And through December 29, 2027, enrolled veterans don’t pay co-pays for their first three outpatient mental health or substance use visits each calendar year, whether those visits happen at a VA facility or with a provider in the VA’s community care network.

If the VA can’t see you close to home or soon enough, you may qualify to see a community provider paid for by the VA. That care generally needs VA authorization before your appointment. Our veteran mental health resources page explains how the Community Care Network works.

Care You May Be Able to Get Without VA Enrollment

Some of the most useful VA mental health services don’t require you to be enrolled first. These are worth knowing about if you haven’t applied yet, if your paperwork is still in progress or if you’ve assumed you don’t qualify.

Vet Centers. These community-based centers offer free, confidential readjustment services to eligible veterans, service members and their families, including many Guard and Reserve members. They operate separately from VA medical centers and don’t require VA health care enrollment.

Emergency suicide care under the COMPACT Act. Eligible veterans in an acute suicidal crisis can go to any VA or non-VA emergency room and the VA will provide or pay for that care, including up to 30 days of inpatient or crisis residential care and up to 90 days of outpatient care. Eligibility depends on service history and discharge status, not VA enrollment. In an emergency, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room first.

Care related to military sexual trauma (MST). The VA provides MST-related mental health care to eligible veterans and former service members, including many with other-than-honorable discharges, even if the experience wasn’t reported at the time.

Mental health care for some former service members with other-than-honorable discharges. The VA makes these decisions case by case, so an other-than-honorable discharge doesn’t automatically rule you out. It’s worth asking.

Using TRICARE and the VA Together

If you’re a military retiree who also qualifies for VA health care, you don’t have to choose one. TRICARE’s guidance is to use the VA for service-connected conditions and TRICARE for everything else. Many retirees enroll in both so they have more options for where and how they get care.

One detail to check: If you have TRICARE For Life, a VA facility isn’t a Medicare provider. Using TRICARE For Life at a VA facility for a non-service-connected condition can leave you with a balance to pay, so ask about costs before your visit. The broader guide to using insurance for mental health treatment can help you compare options.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do Veterans Get TRICARE?

Most don’t. TRICARE generally covers military retirees, including those who retired for medical reasons, along with active duty service members, their families and some Guard and Reserve members. Some people who leave service get up to 180 days of transitional TRICARE coverage. Veterans who separated without retiring usually get mental health care through the VA instead.

Is VA Health Care the Same as Insurance?

No. The VA is a health care system that provides care directly through its own facilities and, when needed, pays for care from approved community providers. That’s why the first step with the VA is usually enrolling, not finding an in-network provider.

Do I Need a Referral to See a Therapist With TRICARE?

It depends on your status and plan. Active duty members need a referral and pre-authorization for civilian network care but not for outpatient care at a military hospital or clinic. Family members on TRICARE Prime generally don’t need a referral for office-based outpatient therapy with a network provider, and TRICARE Select enrollees don’t need one for most outpatient care.

Can I Use TRICARE and the VA at the Same Time?

Yes, if you qualify for both, which is most common for military retirees. The VA handles service-connected conditions and TRICARE covers other care.

Find the Right Starting Point

Military health benefits come with their own language, and it’s easy to put off care while you try to sort out which system applies. You don’t have to have every answer before you reach out. Knowing your status and your first step is enough to get moving.

The Mental Health Hotline can help you understand your options and find mental health resources, whether you’re using TRICARE, the VA or other coverage. We don’t verify eligibility or process TRICARE or VA referrals, but we can help you figure out where to look next. Call 866-903-3787. It’s free, confidential and available 24/7. If you need immediate support, the Veterans Crisis Line is available by calling 988 and pressing 1 or texting 838255.
